explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus tells His disciples, "You know that the Passover is two days away…" He says it right alongside the news that the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified. The clock is ticking, and Jesus is the one who names the days.

Pentecost is a real day in Scripture, and Acts 2:1 shows people gathered for it. It isn't the feast Jesus names here, though. He says, "You know that the Passover is two days away…" Pentecost showed up to the wrong party, baker, but at least it's a real feast.

The Feast of Tabernacles is in the Bible, and Leviticus 23:34 mentions it. But Jesus doesn't name it here. He tells His disciples, "You know that the Passover is two days away…" Hold onto that date, because it's the one Jesus gives.

True. Jesus says, "…the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified." In Mark 2:10, Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself, so He is talking about His own road. I think this one is hard to hear.

It's true, and the text is clear about it. Jesus tells His disciples, "…the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified." Jesus uses Son of Man as His name for Himself (Mark 2:10). He is telling them ahead of time what is coming for Him.

explanations.answer: Arrest Him covertly and kill Him
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says they "…conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him." Covertly means quietly, out of sight. And they plot it in the courtyard of the high priest, Caiaphas.

That's not what the text says they plan. Matthew 26:4 says they "…conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him." The plan the verse reports is arresting Him quietly and killing Him. Driving Him out of Jerusalem isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: Debate Him in front of the crowds
explanations.explanation: Debating in the open isn't the plan in this passage. The text says they "…conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him." The word covertly means they want it quiet, which is the opposite of a stage in front of a crowd. The next verse shows what they are worried about.

explanations.answer: There may be a riot among the people
explanations.explanation: That's it. They say, "But not during the feast… or there may be a riot among the people." The text gives the riot as their reason. That's the worry behind the condition.

explanations.answer: The courts will be closed for the feast
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions the courts closing. The plotters give their reason in their own words: "or there may be a riot among the people." It's the crowd they are worried about, not a schedule. Courts closing is a good guess, but it's not in this passage.

explanations.answer: Caiaphas will be busy at the temple
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the passage says Caiaphas has plans at the temple. The reason they give is, "or there may be a riot among the people." Caiaphas is the high priest, and the plotters met in his courtyard. But their worry in this verse is the people, and that's the answer.

Yes, baker. The woman came with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, "…which she poured on His head as He reclined at the table." The text puts it right on His head. Hold onto that detail, because Jesus will say what it means.

Close, but the text says head, not hands. Matthew 26:7 says she "…poured on His head as He reclined at the table." It's an easy slip, since hands are where we usually put things like perfume. This woman goes straight to His head.

Shoulders is a fair guess, but the verse says head. She came with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, "…which she poured on His head as He reclined at the table." Me with a full jar of expensive perfume? I'd be so nervous I'd hit the table. She pours it right where the verse says, on His head.
Yes, baker. The disciples "were indignant" and then they ask, "Why this waste?" Indignant means they were upset at what they saw. The text then says Jesus was "Aware of this…"

The text doesn't say they were amazed. It says, "When the disciples saw this, they were indignant…" Indignant means they were upset. Then they asked, "Why this waste?" That's a very different mood from amazed.

The text doesn't mention any tears from the disciples. They "were indignant" and then they ask, "Why this waste?" Indignant means upset, not touched. I think they were looking at that perfume and picturing what else it could have done.

This one is false, and the details matter. The disciples say, "This perfume could have been sold at a high price, and the money given to the poor." They don't mention the temple at all. Their idea is that the money goes to the poor.

Right, baker, it's false. The disciples say, "This perfume could have been sold at a high price, and the money given to the poor." In their words, the money goes to the poor, not the temple. That comes right after they ask, "Why this waste?"
That's the word. Jesus says, "Why are you bothering this woman? She has done a beautiful deed to Me." The disciples are looking at the cost. Jesus looks at the deed and calls it beautiful.

Brave sounds good, but it isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, "She has done a beautiful deed to Me." He is answering the disciples' complaint, and the word He picks is beautiful. I'd have said messy, honestly, but He sees it better than I do.

Quiet is a sneaky guess, I'll give you that. But Jesus says, "She has done a beautiful deed to Me." The disciples called it waste, and Jesus calls it beautiful. That's a big gap between two opinions of one jar.

That's backwards, baker. Jesus says, "The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me." So it's the poor who will be with them, and Jesus who won't always be. This statement flips the two around, which is why it's false.

Right, it's false. Jesus says, "The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me." The poor are the ones who will always be with them. Jesus is the one they will not always have.

That's it. Jesus says, "By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial." Jesus Himself tells them what her deed was for. I think that gives it a weight the disciples hadn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: Anointed Him as king of Israel
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that here. He says, "By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial." Pouring perfume on someone's head is a big gesture, so I see why the guess comes up. But burial is the word Jesus uses.

explanations.answer: Refreshed Him for the road ahead
explanations.explanation: That's a kind guess, but it's not what Jesus says. He tells them, "By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial." The text gives Jesus' own explanation, so we don't need to guess. Her deed was for His burial.

explanations.answer: Her deed will be told wherever the gospel is preached
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, "Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her." She poured out one jar at one table, and Jesus says it will be told in all the world. And here we are telling it.

explanations.answer: Her jar will be paid back to her many times over
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't promise anything like a payback. He says, "Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her." The promise is that her deed will be remembered and told. It has nothing to do with getting the jar back.

explanations.answer: Her name will be written on the walls of the temple
explanations.explanation: Nothing about temple walls in this passage. Jesus says, "Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her." The promise is about her deed being told, wherever the gospel goes. Walls and names aren't part of it.

True. Judas, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests and asked, "What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?" He is the one who brings it up. The chief priests answer by setting out silver.

It's true, and the text is plain about it. Judas went to the chief priests and asked, "What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?" So the question comes from Judas himself, and the chief priests are the ones he asks.

That's the number. The text says, "And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver." Judas asked what they were willing to give, and that was what they set out for him. The chief priests are the ones who set it out.

Twenty isn't the number in the text. Matthew 26:15 says, "And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver." It's an easy one to mix up, since the numbers are close together. The verse says thirty, and that's what the chief priests set out for Judas.

Forty is a little too high. Matthew 26:15 says, "And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver." The chief priests are the ones who set out the silver, after Judas asked what they were willing to give. The number the text gives is thirty.
